title: The Fathers on Numbers
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The law enrolled only those twenty and older because what is vigorous and in its prime is fit for God's book, making bodily age a sketch of spiritual age.
comments.comment: The common people were enrolled from twenty years old and upward (Numbers 1:3), because the exactness of the law did not, I think, consider what was still feeble and powerless worthy to be written in God’s book. For what is vigorous and already in its spiritual prime would rightly be admitted to the lists of the saints. So the law makes bodily age an apt sketch of spiritual age: it set down as chosen those in their prime, passing over the beardless, the weak and the still boyish, and not entering them in the sacred book.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the enrollment began at twenty years old.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Only the fully grown male of twenty is enrolled in God's book, and Moses and Aaron together show the one Christ.
comments.comment: That therefore the male and most fight-ready, and having gone up unto youth—that is, unto the spiritual good condition and unto a measure of stature of Christ’s fullness—has been set in the divine enrollment, and in God’s book, would become clear also through these things very well; for the male having come to be in a twentieth and still year is numbered for no other reason, as I think, than so that we ourselves also may be able to understand that the strengthless and incomplete unto understanding is cast away and unapproved … And the things of the enrollment were being practiced through both Moses and Aaron, so that through both we may understand the one Christ, as in Moses lawgiver, as in Aaron high priest.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: The whole people were counted so that those joined to God might know they are in his registers, while the tribe of Levi was set apart from the count.
comments.comment: That the Levitical tribe is chosen and set apart from the others he makes plain in this way. He commanded the common people to be counted and an exact reckoning to be made of the general multitude, not because the Creator did not know. For the drops of rain are numbered by him, as it is written (Job 36:27), and nothing could escape that pure mind. He did it so that those who read the sacred Scriptures might know very clearly that those who are joined to God and bear the name of his people go into the registers kept with God and into the book of life, are counted among those he knows, and are already in the remembrance of the Master of all. So the common people were enrolled; but God set the chosen and holy tribe apart, as it were, by itself, and in no way let it stand in equal rank with the others, but reserved for it, as it were, the foremost portion, saying to Moses, wisest of men: ‘As for the tribe of Levi, see that you do not include their number in the count, nor take it among the sons of Israel’ (Numbers 1:49). For the lot of the holy is set apart, and their honors are of the highest.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Levi is left out of the count.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Judah's camp holds the first place because Christ comes from Judah, so those in Christ are honored ahead of the firstborn and the free in faith ahead of those from slavery.
comments.comment: Do you see that Judah and those with him are placed first, and hold the chosen place toward the dawn and the south? For those who are in Christ are in the light, and fervent in the Spirit (Romans 12:11). Second comes Reuben and those with him. Third, again, are the sons of the free woman. Then after them come three others, the sons of the maidservants, of whom it is said, ‘They shall set out last’ (Numbers 2:31). Is it not plain, and in no way open to doubt, that the second, that is, the people in Christ, has been honoured above the firstborn and called in ahead of it, and so have those who are free in faith above those who come from slavery? For the one group leads because of Christ, who is from Judah; the others only barely follow behind, and have been placed, as it were, in the second rank.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the order of the camps means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The Levites serve as helpers to those who perform the sacred rites.
comments.comment: [The] Levites have been assigned as fellow workers, in a way, and helpers, as it were, to those who perform the sacred rites. For ‘they shall keep his charges’ (meaning, clearly, Aaron’s) ‘and all the furnishings of the tent of witness, and the charges of the sons of Israel’ (Numbers 3:7–8). Their share in the work goes this far.
comments.selected_reason: Plain account of the Levites' helping role.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: The law sketched the order of the Church in advance: bishops and presbyters keep the altar and what is within the veil, and deacons keep the charges of the tent.
comments.comment: And if anyone should choose to look closely at the order of the Church as well, he would rightly marvel at the way the law sketched it in advance. For to the bishops, since it has fallen to them to preside, and also to those who hold the lesser rank (I mean the presbyters), the altar and the things within the veil have been entrusted; and these words would fit them: ‘And they shall keep their priesthood’ (Numbers 3:10). To the deacons belongs: ‘They shall keep the charges of the tent, and all its furnishings, and the charges of the people’ (Numbers 3:7–8). Or is it not they who call out in the churches and direct the people, now to sing hymns as is fitting, now to stand in good order, often to keep silence? Do they not rouse them to prayer, and, when the bloodless sacrifice is being offered, themselves bring forward the more sacred vessels and keep careful watch over everything needed?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Aaron and his sons are set over the tent and the altar, a type of Christ appointed over his house, with the apostles as his fellow workers.
comments.comment: But he sets over the tent both Aaron and his sons with him; for ‘they shall keep,’ he says, ‘their own priesthood and all that concerns the altar, and the things within the veil’ (Numbers 3:10), that is, the secret and more mystical things, and all that those who wait on the divine altar are accustomed to do. And the type, in its pure sense, points to Christ, whom the Father appointed over his house, whose house we are (Hebrews 3:6). And those who share the priesthood with Aaron would signify, clearly enough, the sacred and admirable company of the holy apostles, who work and minister, as it were, together with Christ. For they have become God’s fellow workers (1 Corinthians 3:9), treasurers and stewards of the mysteries of God (1 Corinthians 4:1), and also ministers through whom we have believed (1 Corinthians 3:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who keeps the priesthood and what it points to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: The law set apart the tribe of Levi as a type pointing to us, who are a chosen race and enter the truer tent, the Church.
comments.comment: In just this way the law, of course, sketched in shadow for the people of old this same life, so worthy of reverence and so well worth gaining, when it commanded them to slaughter sheep, to make their offerings by means of blood, to dedicate tithes and firstfruits to God, and thank offerings besides. Yet it laid down that these things must not be done outside the holy tent. And it set apart the tribe of Levi as chosen and dedicated to God (Numbers 3:12), making the thing a type given to us and pointing to ourselves. For we too are called in the divine Scriptures ‘a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession’ (1 Peter 2:9). And we enter the truer tent, which the Lord pitched and not man (Hebrews 8:2), that is, the Church; not appeasing the Maker of all things with calves and goats (Hebrews 9:12), but excelling in a right and blameless faith, and giving off, in a spiritual way, a sweet fragrance through spiritual offerings of fruit. ‘For with such sacrifices God is well pleased’ (Hebrews 13:16), and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth, as the Savior said (John 4:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the setting apart of Levi means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The Levites were enrolled from a month old because the Master gladly accepts the childlikeness in Christ of those he has chosen, along with good sense.
comments.comment: But for the Levites the enrollment was from a month old (Numbers 3:15). For the Master of all very gladly accepts the childlikeness in Christ of those he has chosen, just as, of course, he accepts good sense. For to excel in both, I mean in understanding and in the simplicity that is in Christ, is exceptional. Indeed, the inspired Paul says: ‘Brothers, do not be children in your thinking; be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature’ (1 Corinthians 14:20). And Christ himself says somewhere: ‘Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves’ (Matthew 10:16). So the simplicity of the saints is acceptable. And the numbering was by name, and also by clans and fathers’ houses. For God grants his own watchful care to those whom he chooses to honor, one by one, as a multitude, and by family. And the Savior himself makes plain how exact this is, when he says to the holy apostles: ‘Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father who is in heaven. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered’ (Matthew 10:29–30).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Levites were counted from a month old.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Israel was called among the first, but when the Gentiles ran in between it was ranked after them, so the last became first and the first last.
comments.comment: In the first census of the Levites, those of Gershon were placed at the head, then Kohath in the middle, and last Merari; these are the Levitical clans (Numbers 3:17). But in the second census, the one counted from twenty-five years of age, Kohath is set before the others and named first (Numbers 4:2–3). After him, and last, come Gershon and Merari, whose service is the extra things of the tent (Numbers 4:22–33). Each of these two clans has only two families, while Kohath extends to as many as four (Numbers 3:18–20). Do you grasp the riddle, then? … Israel was called among the first; but when the flock of the Gentiles ran in between, Israel was ranked after it. And so the last have become first, as the Savior said, and the first last (Matthew 20:16). … And it is plain that the Jewish people are few in number, while the countless multitude from the Gentiles far exceeds them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Only the age fixed by the law, twenty-five to fifty, was assigned to the sacred tasks, because the sensible and strong render God a service beyond reproach.
comments.comment: But that only the age fixed by the law, from twenty-five to fifty years (Numbers 4:3), was assigned to the sacred tasks shows, I think, that all who are sensible and strong, both those who are already so and those who are still so, render to God a service that is choice and beyond reproach. For the man who has reached twenty-five years is already among them, and the man who has gone on as far as fifty is still among them. For a man who has passed beyond his fiftieth year has in some way already begun to decline toward the end of his strength. He is no longer in the flawless prime of life, but is creeping, as it were, toward the ailments of old age. No one unwise, and no one feeble, could serve God without fault, if it is true to say that whatever looks toward virtue is the work of strength and of an excellent mind; and it has fallen to these to receive from the Lawgiver the praise that is their due.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Levites served between twenty-five and fifty.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Those of Kohath serve in the most holy things while the priests go in ahead of them, for what ranks first in order is held in greater honor.
comments.comment: To those of the clan of Kohath belongs the service of the most holy things, while the priests go in ahead of them and cover these things (Numbers 4:4–5). For everywhere what ranks first in order is held in greater honor, and all that is with God is in good order; nothing at all is without order. The Levitical order serves in the assisting tasks, placed beneath the sacred ministries of those set above it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the order of service in the tent.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: The blue of the coverings signifies what is from above, the table's purple a sign of Christ's kingship, the scarlet a type of blood, and the laver holy baptism.
comments.comment: …the blue signifying for us what is from above and from heaven. For that is the color of the upper air, high and deep above us. That the sacred vessels are types of Christ, who is from above and from heaven, we have already shown at length. The table, besides its blue wrappings, also has a cloth of pure purple; the altar of burnt offerings has a scarlet cloth; and the laver too has a cloth of pure purple over its blue coverings. The table, on which the loaves are set out, signifies the bloodless sacrifice, through which we are blessed as we eat the bread from heaven (John 6:51), that is, Christ. He became as we are, yet even so he was and is God, coming from above and from the Father, and above all things (John 3:31), as King and Lord of the universe. And the royal purple cloth spread over the table, that is, the purple wrapping, would be, as it seems to me, a sign of Christ’s kingship. The altar of burnt offerings was clothed in a scarlet cloth, and we shall take the cloth dyed scarlet as a type of blood. For Christ was sacrificed for our sake and on our behalf (1 Corinthians 5:7), and like a lamb he went up onto the divine altar, as a fragrant offering to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2). The laver’s covering, besides the blue, is a cloth of pure purple. The laver bears in itself the type of holy baptism, which washes us in holy waters for the putting away of sin and carries us into the kingdom of heaven. Holy baptism is from above and from heaven, and the blue color hints at this.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Gershon and Merari hint at the peoples under the law and carry the extra things, while the Kohathites, holy in Christ, carry the things through which Christ is signified.
comments.comment: The two clans, Gershon and Merari, seem to hint at the peoples under the law, I mean Israel, and the Kohathites at those sanctified in Christ through faith. The former had in their care the hangings of the court, the hide curtains of the tent, the coverings and the pillars, the capitals and the bases, the pegs and the screens, and, as Holy Scripture says, ‘all the extra things’ (Numbers 4:26), by which is meant what is not essential in the service. The Kohathites were entrusted with carrying the most holy things, the things through which Christ is signified, not in a single way, but rather in many ways and many forms: as the ark, as the table, as the golden lampstand, and as the golden altar of incense. For though he is simple by nature, as God, he is made known in many ways through the variety of his works. For the Word of the Father is, as all confess, living and active (Hebrews 4:12), and besides this he is life and light (John 1:4), and the scent of a spiritual fragrance. So those who devote themselves to the commandments given through Moses have the extra things of the tent as their service, for the law is of no use unless it is understood spiritually. But those entrusted with the most holy things are surely holy in Christ. They carry nothing extra, but bear, as it were, Emmanuel himself seated upon them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the extra things and the most holy things signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: The law's rules on bodily conditions are an image of the diseases of souls, since a bodily affliction no one chooses could not justly bring the law's condemnation.
comments.comment: Now it is clear to anyone, I think, that the law could not reasonably be thought to rebuke us in these matters for what happens by necessity and against our will. For why should a bodily affliction be punished, and how could the one who has fallen into fleshly infirmities justly incur the law’s condemnation? It is wise, then, and necessary to take these bodily conditions as an image and type of the diseases in souls. For in this way the law would be spiritual (Romans 7:14), and what God has declared on each matter at various times would be a holy verdict, not subjecting to penalties those caught by diseases they did not choose, but those in whose case the fact of wrongdoing would make the rebuke holy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the camp laws on uncleanness are read as types of soul diseases.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Sending the sick out from the company of the saints is not savage temper but a wise safeguard, since a little leaven leavens the whole lump.
comments.comment: You are right, since he [the Lord] counts the sick man hateful, and indeed casts him off, and sends him away from the company of the saints. The inspired Paul understood this very well when he wrote: ‘Drive out, then, the wicked person from among you’ (1 Corinthians 5:13). And I would not call this the fruit of a savage temper, but a wise safeguard. ‘For a little leaven,’ he says, ‘leavens the whole lump’ (1 Corinthians 5:6). And again, the sacred law sketched this for us in a riddle. For it is written in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper, and everyone who has a discharge, and everyone who is unclean through a dead body. Male and female alike, send them outside the camp, and they shall not defile their camps, in which I dwell among them. And the sons of Israel did so’ (Numbers 5:1–4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the unclean are sent out of the camp.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: A man with a discharge was banished from the camp with the lepers because he made unclean anyone he touched or who came near him.
comments.comment: Besides this, the law says that every article on which the man with a discharge sits will be loathsome and abhorred, and that even if he washes his hands in water, that too will be defiled (Leviticus 15:9–11). If anyone touches his skin, he will certainly share in the charge of uncleanness; and if any who are not yet defiled come near him, they will certainly incur the charge of uncleanness. That is why he went out together with the lepers and was banished from the camp (Numbers 5:2), unapproachable and cut off from others, defiling anyone at all who met him by the mere touch of his hand.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Christ welcomes the cleansed but sends the defiled out of the camp of the saints.
comments.comment: For you have learned that Emmanuel, who is God by nature, our great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), counts our affairs worthy of the closest oversight. He welcomes those who have washed away what is evil, but sends out of the camp of the saints those he sees to be defiled (Numbers 5:2–3).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The woman suspected of adultery brings barley meal without oil or frankincense, a sign of a beastlike life, while the gifts of those not under suspicion are fine wheat flour with frankincense and oil.
comments.comment: He commanded that the woman suspected of adultery, when she faces a charge that has no proofs, be brought to the priest and stand in the sight of God (Numbers 5:15–16); and this, I think, means that all are going to stand before Christ (Romans 14:10). Next, he commanded that the gift offered for her be barley meal, not sprinkled with frankincense, not moistened with oil; for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, which brings sin to remembrance (Numbers 5:15). It is plain, then, that from each person’s life a kind of odor, as it were, rises up to God: against those who have let themselves slide into carelessness it brings the charge of every monstrous deed, but for those who have striven earnestly to live rightly and well it bears witness to their genuineness. That is why we say, and with very good reason, that the gifts of those who are not under suspicion consist of fine wheat flour, with frankincense added and oil poured over it (Leviticus 2:1). For it will surely follow that a life which stays human, of which the fine wheat flour would also be a type, must be reckoned as fragrance and gladness before God, who loves virtue. But barley meal would be a very clear sign of a spurious and beastlike life. For to be unrestrained in appetite, and to want to rush without a bridle into monstrous pleasures, is somehow more fitting for cattle, and not at all becoming to a human being. That is why the woman accused of a spurious life brought barley meal to God without frankincense and oil, that is, without fragrance and gladness; for it is a sacrifice that brings sin to remembrance. And where sin is brought to remembrance, how or from where could gladness come? For the one on trial is not in hope of crowns, but in fear of punishment and fire.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the suspected woman's offering is barley meal without oil or frankincense.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The woman is brought to the judge with her head uncovered because the charge is unseemliness, and also because all things are naked before the eyes of the Judge.
comments.comment: Besides this, the woman is brought to the judge with her head uncovered (Numbers 5:18), that is, not in her usual and fitting adornment. And what would be the reason for this? The charges are of unseemliness, and the indictment is for shameless conduct. Remember that Paul, who was learned in the law, does not allow a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered (1 Corinthians 11:5), and takes the law of nature (1 Corinthians 11:14) as his proof that she must be covered: ‘For her hair,’ he says, ‘is given to her as a covering.’ (1 Corinthians 11:15) So the woman, accused of unseemliness, was no longer in seemly adornment. But she is uncovered in another sense too. For all things are naked before the eyes of the Judge (Hebrews 4:13), and no one at all could escape the notice of him who searches hearts and inward parts (Psalm 7:9), who also says through the voice of the prophet: ‘I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?’ (Jeremiah 23:23–24)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the woman's head is uncovered.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The law bars the consecrated person from going near the dead, even a father or mother, so that God holds the first place over kinship by blood.
comments.comment: Let the mind, then, be filled with thoughts that lead to rightness, and be crowned, as with a head of hair, with the discoveries of reflection on everything admirable. Such a person is as sensible as can be, and well fitted from now on to receive into himself the enlightenment that is in Christ through faith. As for the one so well endowed, who has trained himself in an exceptional life and is distinguished by such a mind, the divine oracle commands him to keep far from everything that by its nature defiles, to withdraw from fleshly deeds, and to cast as far away as possible whatever tends toward deadness and corruption. So the rule that one must not visit the dead, nor be willing to be defiled over a corpse, surely hints at this for us. The law bars him from such things entirely, setting what pleases God above reverence for parents. ‘For he shall not go near,’ it says, ‘his father or his mother’ (Numbers 6:6–7). For when virtue is being achieved, away with love of the flesh; let God hold the first and higher place over kinship by blood. This is what Christ himself also said: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:37–38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Nazirite may not go near his dead parents.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Israel, who vowed to keep the law, must shave off the teaching of the law like hair and grow it again after the eighth day, the day of Christ's resurrection.
comments.comment: So then, before the coming of the Savior, Israel was called through Moses to the knowledge of God, and for this reason he was also sanctified. And in a certain way he made to God the vow of purity. For at Mount Horeb he plainly promised that he would keep the law, saying: ‘All that the Lord God has spoken we will do and hear’ (Exodus 24:7; Deuteronomy 5:27). So his mind was full of the teaching of the law, and the glories of the commandment given through Moses were, as it were, a head of hair grown for God. But they were defiled by a dead body, for they killed Emmanuel. The death of Christ was truly holy, but for those who killed him the guilt of killing the Lord was a defilement. So the law now commands them to shave off the teaching of the law like a head of hair, and, one might almost say, to crop off on the seventh day whatever was in types (Numbers 6:9), that is, whatever came before the eighth day, the day on which Christ came back to life, renewing us to incorruption and refashioning us for a new life, the life of the Gospel. So, having cropped off what came before the eighth day, he grows his hair again and sanctifies his head after the eighth day (Numbers 6:11). And the mind grows its hair again no longer with types and shadows, as before, but with the very teachings that stand in faith and truth. Or do you not think that those justified by faith must be stripped, as it were, of the good repute won by worship under the law, and must grow anew and take into their inmost mind and heart the knowledge of the Gospel way of life, as far better and more excellent than the way given at the beginning?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: A consecrated person defiled by a dead body loses the days already served, but is scoured clean in Christ, whom the birds and the lamb foreshadow.
comments.comment: But if it should happen, it says, that the consecrated person is ever defiled over a dead body, let him then be shorn and have his head stripped bare, since his hair has now in a way become unholy. And on the eighth day he shall bring a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. And let him also bring, it says, a year-old lamb; and the first days shall not count, because the head of his vow was defiled (Numbers 6:9–12). For if the consecrated person should grow careless of what is fitting and be defiled by ways that lead to deadness, having turned aside to the things of the flesh, it will surely follow that he must barter away the glories of the wholly pure way of life, and he will make his own head, as it were, utterly dishonored. For the shaving hints at something of this kind. And having labored in vain through the time that is past, he will lament the loss of his sweat. This, I think, is the meaning of ‘The first days shall not count.’ … So if the consecrated should somehow be defiled in the meantime, they will suffer the loss of what they had already achieved; yet the loss they suffer from it is not hard to escape. For they are scoured clean in Christ, who, in the place, as it were, of the turtledove and the dove, offers himself for us to God the Father, and is sacrificed as a lamb, and justifies us by the death of his own flesh. That is why the law has ordered that the one who has undergone the shaving should offer sacrifices as a type of Christ, who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), strengthens what is weak, raises what has fallen, turns back what has strayed (Ezekiel 34:16), and washes clean what has been stained.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The turtledove and dove sign Christ as sweet-voiced and gentle, and the lamb shows him from the earth below as the birds show him from above.
comments.comment: So the riddle shows that the teaching of the law has become idle. It commands Israel, who had made the vow, to be shaved as one who had incurred defilement from a dead body, that is, as one held fast in the guilt of killing the Lord; and to sanctify to God, as it were, another head of hair after the eighth day, that is, after the resurrection: the precise and finely wrought refinement and teaching of the decrees of the Gospel. To the one who grows his hair after the eighth day the law prescribed the offering of turtledoves and doves (Numbers 6:10), setting this down too as a sign of the one who cleanses the defiled, that is, of Christ. For he is signified by both: as most sweet-voiced by the turtledove, as most gentle by the dove; whereas the law is slow of tongue (Exodus 4:10) and has no gentleness, for it punishes wrongdoers at once. A lamb is also offered together with the birds (Numbers 6:12), so that Christ may be understood through them all: through the birds as from above and from heaven, through the lamb as from below and from the earth. For the Word, who is God by nature, became flesh (John 1:14). Yet even so he was and is God. He frees us from the shadow of the law and puts into the hearts of all the knowledge of his own decrees; and he makes us truly holy, cleansing us with his own blood, according to the Scriptures (Hebrews 13:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the birds and the lamb of the offering signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The lamb stands for childlikeness in Christ, the ram for maturity, the ewe lamb for the need of cleansing even in the purified, and the loaves and wafers for a pure and sweet life.
comments.comment: By the lamb we may fitly understand the childlikeness in Christ of the one who brings the sacrifice, and by the ram what is mature in mind and, as it were, in bearing fruit. For he says: ‘Brothers, do not be children in your minds; rather, be infants in evil, but in your minds be mature’ (1 Corinthians 14:20). Between them stands the ewe lamb, offered for sin. Through this again it is easier for us to see that even the life of those who are thoroughly purified, who live, as it were, in the simplicity and innocence understood in Christ and have been made perfect in soundness of mind, is not wholly without blame, but certainly needs cleansing. For no one will possess what is wholly beyond reproach. It is reserved for Emmanuel alone, and will remain his own, to say in truth: ‘For the ruler of this age is coming, and he will find nothing in me’ (John 14:30). So in the lamb, the ewe lamb and the ram one may see what I have said. In the unleavened loaves the sincere and pure life is signified; for the most wise Paul writes somewhere to the sanctified: ‘So clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened’ (1 Corinthians 5:7). And in the wafer is the savor, and as it were the sweetness, of the life of the saints.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what each offering in the Nazirite's gift signifies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: With Christ as mediator we offer prayers for our sins, are offered whole to God, and bring thank offerings of a pure, unleavened life.
comments.comment: That is why the oil was rightly poured on the loaves. The priest again acts as mediator, and brings first the sin offering, then the whole burnt offering, and third, after these, the ram of the peace offering (Numbers 6:16–17). For with Christ mediating and bringing us to God the Father, we shall be accepted as we bring prayers for our own sins and ask forgiveness for our former offenses. We are also offered as whole burnt offerings in a spiritual sense, that is, entirely and completely, holy and consecrated, and we shall be dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma, not divided toward the things of the world; for the whole burnt offering was consumed entire by the fire. We shall also dedicate thank offerings for our own salvation and life, honoring God not with perishable and earthly things, but bringing him, as it were, a guest’s gift fit to be accepted: a life that is pure and unleavened, sweet and holy; for such, in some way, is the life of the saints.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of the sin offering, whole burnt offering and peace offering.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The priests bless the people, yet it is not a human hand that blesses but the Lord himself, whose gifts come through Christ.
comments.comment: So he commands those crowned with the priesthood to bless the people, but he usefully keeps them from rash thinking by showing that it is not a human hand that blesses, but he himself, as Lord. For ‘every good gift and every good present and every blessing is from above, coming down from the Father of lights,’ as it is written (James 1:17). And Christ is the way of the blessing; he is the one who distributes the heavenly goods to us, and in him and through him all things come from the Father. Indeed the inspired Paul says, ‘Grace to you and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 1:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who really gives the priestly blessing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The threefold naming of the Lord in the blessing shows three persons.
comments.comment: In order to show three persons, he did not say once: “the Lord bless you and shine upon you and give you peace,” but a third time he named him “Lord.”
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: On the Trinity

comments.capsule: The blessing keeps us by undoing the curse.
comments.comment: The blessing, then, keeps us, for it undoes the curse and refashions what had sinned, so that in Christ it may be found worthy of praise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The oxen brought in pairs under one yoke are a type of the two peoples running together under the yoke of the Savior with endurance and courage.
comments.comment: Each leader also gave an ox, twelve in all. They carry the holy tent as their load, brought in pairs to a single wagon and under a single yoke, and they were assigned to the service of the Levites (Numbers 7:3–6). This would be a type of the two peoples, no longer divided by unlike doctrines and ways of life, but brought together and, as it were, running together under the one yoke of the Savior (Matthew 11:29), with endurance and courage. For it says: ‘Be courageous, and let your heart be strong, and wait for the Lord’ (Psalm 27:14). And the ox is an animal that endures hardship and is very strong. Such, surely, are those who have chosen godliness: they carry Christ upon themselves like a yoke, as the one prefigured in the holy tent. The divine Paul, too, called the Church his body (Colossians 1:24). And it was said to Ananias about him, I mean about Paul: ‘Go, for this man is a chosen vessel to me, to carry my name before the Gentiles’ (Acts 9:15).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The calves were given for the work of the tent so that the camp's loads would be carried on wagons, as the Church rests upon Christ, who carries us.
comments.comment: Notice, too, that the calves were brought, but were given for the work of the tent, so that when the camp moved they might carry the loads on wagons and spare those who performed the sacred service toil and distress (Numbers 7:3–8). For the Church rests upon Christ, and he carries us. He does not let the holy and precious race, the people skilled in holy works, fall into labours beyond their strength. In this way, then, the things named must be referred to Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the leaders' gifts were wagons and animals for carrying.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The law is a heavy load, so the extra things are not carried on shoulders, but the Kohathites make of the things signifying Christ a light load, easy to carry.
comments.comment: This, my friend, I would say: the law is burdensome, a load hard to bear. And a clear sign of this would be that the extra things are not carried on the shoulders, because those under the yoke are weak. That is why the inspired disciples said to those who, after coming to faith, were turning to the worship of the law: ‘Now therefore why are you putting God to the test, by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither you nor your fathers were able to bear?’ (Acts 15:10) But the Kohathites set on their own shoulders the things by which Christ is signified, and make of them a light load, easy to carry. Is this not plainly what Christ himself said: ‘My yoke is easy, and my burden is light’? (Matthew 11:30)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Kohathites carry the holy things on their shoulders.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: The leaders came in a mystical order showing that what comes through Christ holds first rank over what belongs to the law, with Judah, from whom Christ sprang, bringing his gift first.
comments.comment: When they came forward with their gifts, Palladius, they did not come by age. First came Judah, though he was fourth in time (Numbers 7:12–17); after him Issachar, the ninth son, and with them Zebulun, the tenth (Numbers 7:18–29). After these came a second company, as it were: Reuben the firstborn, and Simeon, the next and second son (Numbers 7:30–41). Dan, a slave woman’s son, was joined to them as well. Next came a third rank, made up of three freeborn sons: Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin (Numbers 7:48–65). The fourth company, at the very end, is made up of those born of the servant women. These again are three, Dan, Asher and Naphtali (Numbers 7:66–83), although in the time of their birth they come before those placed ahead of them in order, I mean Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin. Would you not say this calls for close examination? … The matter is a riddle, I think, once again. It shows that what comes through Christ holds the first rank with God over what belongs to the law, and that the first have been made last and the last first (Matthew 19:30). For those older in time, and for that reason firstborn, that is, Israel, come behind the Gentiles. And those who have the spirit of slavery (Romans 8:15), the sons of the Jerusalem that is in slavery, will yield the first place in glory to the sons of the free woman, who is the mother of us who have been justified in Christ (Galatians 4:25–26) and called to the dignity of the free through the Spirit of freedom. Look, if you will, at how exact these insights are. The tribe of Judah brings its gift first (Numbers 7:12), the tribe from which Christ sprang according to the flesh (Hebrews 7:14). Right after it come Issachar and Zebulun, both free and born of free parents.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The leaders' offering of fruit hints at Christ, offered in many ways and on every day, and at us who die to the world and live to God.
comments.comment: The thing is an offering of fruit, Palladius; but woven into it, I think, is also a mystical meaning, which refers the riddle to Emmanuel and to ourselves. I will explain it again as well as I can. Now that the holy and true tent (Hebrews 8:2), that is, the Church, has been revealed in this world, Christ, shining out in it in many ways, is offered, one might almost say, by us and on our behalf, as a sacred victim to God the Father, a ransom and exchange for the life of all, the One who is worth as much as all. For since the Only-begotten became man as one of us, he offered himself to God the Father (Ephesians 5:2), as a kind of first offering and firstfruits of human nature, fragrant with holiness: a holiness that is his by nature and in essence, inasmuch as he is understood to be God and is God, but that is his in turn as something received, because of his humanity. And though he is one, he was depicted in many ways, as in the offering of the leaders; and so too, even now, Christ is offered in sacrifice through those who serve as leaders in each age, being understood in many ways and honored with various names. The offering each day suggests, in a way, that the sacrifice of Christ never fails and never ceases on any day, and that those who have been justified by faith bear fruit in it. For worshippers will not fail, nor will there be any lack of gifts. Christ will be offered by us and on our behalf, mystically sacrificed in the holy tents. He himself is our first and choicest offering of fruit; for he offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father, not for himself, indeed, as irreproachable reasoning holds, but rather for us who were under the yoke and indictment of sin. And in likeness to him we too are sacred victims, dying to the world, since sin has been put to death in us, and living to God (Romans 6:11) the life of holiness and godliness. This, it seems, is what the leaders’ offering hints at for us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The silver dish and cup full of fine flour soaked in oil signify Christ as life and the giver of life.
comments.comment: The gifts from each of the tribal leaders, then, are one silver dish and one cup, both full of fine flour mixed with oil. The dish serves for food and is useful for eating what goes with bread, as the Savior himself showed when he told John, his true disciple, who was eager to learn it, who would betray him: ‘He who dipped his hand in the dish with me,’ he says (Matthew 26:23). And why should I speak of the use of the cup, when the thing itself cries it aloud? Fine flour is a sign of bread, since bread is made from it, and the bread of life is Christ (John 6:35). So in the dish and the cup, as it were, and in the bread that was in both (for both were full of fine flour), as in food and drink, Christ is signified as life and as the giver of life. ‘For truly,’ he says, ‘I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves’ (John 6:53).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the dish, the cup and the fine flour with oil stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The fine flour is a symbol of life and the oil of gladness, while the golden dish of incense depicts the beauty of the saints.
comments.comment: the fine flour is a symbol of life, since bread, which keeps us in life, is made from it; and the oil is a symbol of gladness. So let us too, for our part, offer to God who is over all, through our hope in Christ, the gladness that belongs to a bright life. For it says: ‘Rejoicing in hope’ (Romans 12:12). And how could those who keep the commandments of our Savior, and have trained themselves thoroughly in a life and conduct of shining distinction, not be filled with the highest joy? For them a share in his glory is stored up with God, wholly and surely. For it says: ‘For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you also will be revealed with him in glory’ (Colossians 3:3–4). So the fine flour is mixed with oil (Numbers 7:13). For in the life of the saints there is also the gladness that comes from the hope of glory, together, of course, with the brightness that belongs to holiness and righteousness. And the golden dish full of incense (Numbers 7:14) depicts the beauty of the saints: their fragrance in sanctification, held as in choice vessels, and then, as it were, a gift to God that is truly most fragrant. Or should we not think, Palladius, that the saints are bright and choice vessels?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Christ is both fragrance and censer, and is portrayed in the calf, the ram, the lamb and the male goat.
comments.comment: The incense dish, again, has the shape and form of a censer, being made like a small bowl, and it too is filled with incense. For Christ is both fragrance and censer. He does not have his fragrance from outside, as we ourselves do, who come to have it by sharing in virtue and in the holiness that belongs to godliness. He has it from within, as God, and is rich in his own nature in all for which he is wondered at, and he fills the whole world with a fragrance that is above the world and above creation. For since he is God by nature and in truth, and has in his own nature the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father (2 Corinthians 2:14), he is very clearly recognized for what he is. The incense dish, then, is full of incense. Accordingly there are brought a calf and a ram, and a lamb as well, and a male goat, the offerings brought in addition to these; and through them all he himself is portrayed. In the calf, because of its great strength, and because among the tame and clean animals the calf is foremost, and greatest in size of body; and all that is Christ’s stands in a spiritual pre-eminence, and he himself is the One who excels and stands above, by a difference beyond comparison in every respect whatever. In the ram, because of its full maturity; and in the lamb, because of its innocence: ‘For I,’ he says, ‘like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, did not know’ (Jeremiah 11:19). In the male goat, because of the slaughter on behalf of those who had sinned. For under the law the male goat is the sacrifice for sin; and Emmanuel went down into death for our sake, and we have been redeemed from our ancient offences through the slaughter he endured for us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the incense dish and each animal signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The ram and the lamb hint at the coming to God of the older people and the new, and show the fruit of meekness in those justified by faith.
comments.comment: Besides these, a ram and a lamb were offered (Numbers 7:15). They hint at the coming to God of the older people and of the new, and at their dedication, so to speak, which is plainly a spiritual one. For just as endurance and courage were signified in the oxen, so in the same way, I think, the sheep clearly show the fruit borne in meekness by those who have been justified through faith in Christ. For the animal is gentle, and fruitful as well. Such are all who labor with exactness at the Gospel way of life, to whom Christ himself said: ‘Give to everyone who asks you, and from the one who takes what is yours do not demand it back; and to the one who strikes you on the cheek, turn the other also’ (Luke 6:30; Matthew 5:39).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the ram and the lamb signify.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The whole burnt offering was consumed entire and so fits Christ, who is wholly holy, while the sacrifice of salvation was consecrated only in part, as befits us.
comments.comment: In the whole burnt offerings the animals were burned up entire by the sacred and unquenchable fire, no part at all held back; every portion and every limb rose, as it were, to God as a fragrant aroma. But the animals slaughtered for the sacrifice of salvation received a partial consecration, in the right shoulder, for example, the head and the feet, the kidneys and the liver, and certain other inner parts and entrails. It is fitting, then, that Christ should be offered as a whole burnt offering, for he is truly holy in his entirety, wholly fragrant and sacred. But to us belongs what is not altogether holy and not entirely sacred, for there is some defilement in us too, because of the sin that is in us. For ‘no one is clean from filth’ (Job 14:4), and ‘Who will understand his transgressions?’ (Psalm 19:12), as it is written. For this reason the law very rightly commanded that the sacrifice of salvation be consecrated not as a whole burnt offering, but rather in part.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between the whole burnt offering and the sacrifice of salvation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The goat offering shows that even those of good character need cleansing through repentance, which is now our sacrifice for forgiveness.
comments.comment: That the offering of a goat must follow what has already been named (Numbers 7:16) would show, I think, nothing other than what I said just now: that all people, even any whose settled character is good, need cleansing through repentance and the pardon of their trespasses. Knowing this, the divine David said: ‘If you should mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will stand?’ (Psalm 130:3). Under the old law, then, the goat was the sacrifice for forgiveness. But now repentance and the plea for pardon are the sacrifice for us who draw near to God in spirit and in truth (John 4:23). For it says: ‘State your sins first, that you may be justified’ (Isaiah 43:26). And David too sings somewhere: ‘I said, I will confess my sin against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart’ (Psalm 32:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a goat for sin follows the other offerings.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The calf is Christ our leader, and the heifers are ourselves, yoked beneath him and far less in strength and glory.
comments.comment: As for the animals for the sacrifice of salvation, the leaders brought them, as it were, in place of themselves, consecrating them in some way to the holy tent and offering them up to God as a fragrant aroma. There were two heifers, five rams, five he-goats and five ewe lambs. Now the calf is Christ, and the heifers are we ourselves, and the reasoning about the two is not out of keeping, but rather true and plain. For the male is always, in a way, the one most fitted to lead, and held in the highest honour and glory with God; and nature is witness to it, admitting the fact. The female is lesser and placed beneath, coming as it were behind the strength and glory of the male. So in the male calf Christ is our leader, while we, as it were, are yoked beneath him and far less than he in strength and glory, and the distance between is beyond comparison.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The voice of God came from above the mercy seat, which is the Son, who conveys to us the words that come from the Father.
comments.comment: For when the holy tent had, as it were, been completed, and the true sanctuary, which is the Church, had been shown to the world, then indeed the voice of God the Father came to us. ‘For he has spoken to us in the Son’ (Hebrews 1:2), whom we also call the mercy seat for our sins, according to the Scriptures (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). The voice comes from above the cherubim, for God is above all creation and beyond it, and his supremacy over everything that has come into being belongs to his very essence and is inherent in him. And the Son, the true mercy seat, conveying to us the words that come from above and from the Father, said: ‘The words that I speak are not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 14:10, 24). So the voice came from above the mercy seat.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the voice from above the mercy seat.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The seven lamps facing the front of the lampstand give light to those who stand face to face with God through faith, not to those under his turning away.
comments.comment: Notice, then, that the seven lamps, turned to face the front of the lampstand, sent their light to those who looked on. For the divine and spiritual light does not shine on those who stand behind and lie, as it were, under God’s turning away, but on those who have been brought into his sight through sanctification and now stand face to face with him through boldness in faith and the noble dignity of an upright life. For everything that dwells in wickedness and disobedience is loathsome and hateful, but what is obedient and willing to be guided is precious and under God’s care. For to the Jews, who chose to abuse him without restraint, he also says through the voice of Isaiah, ‘When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you’ (Isaiah 1:15). But ‘the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous’ (Psalm 34:15), as is sung in the Psalms.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the lamps shine toward the front of the lampstand.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The Levites' purification with water is mystical, for Christ is our cleansing, whose blood sanctifies far more than the ashes of a heifer.
comments.comment: It is a mystical one, Palladius, and once again it is in Christ. For he is our cleansing, the washing away of every stain, and the giver of sanctification. ‘For you shall sprinkle them,’ it says, ‘with water of purification’ (Numbers 8:7). This is just what the wise Paul made plain when he wrote: ‘For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who have been defiled, sanctify for the purity of the flesh, how much more the blood of Christ’ (Hebrews 9:13–14). And the saying is true. For if there is benefit in the types, and the shadow brings salvation, how could the truth, that is, the blood of Christ, not do so far more?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the water of purification points to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The razor shows the word of God cutting away the uncleanness of the impulses of the flesh as it grows back, and the washing of garments points to a bright and genuine way of life.
comments.comment:
For this, I think, is shown very clearly by the shaving of the body’s hair with a razor (Numbers 8:7). For ‘the word of God is living and active and sharper…’ (Hebrews 4:12), and it cuts away from the mind, as one would hair and nails, the uncleanness of the impulses of the flesh that are inborn in us. Holy Scripture somewhere calls this a law of sin dwelling in the members of the flesh, waging war against the law of the mind, and dragging us toward what is forbidden (Romans 7:23). But cut as with a razor by the power and working of the Holy Spirit, it grows weak, and even if it somehow springs up again in us, it is all the more quickly shorn away. For, ‘walk by the Spirit,’ he says, ‘and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh’ (Galatians 5:16).

Just as the razor does not tear our hair out from the very root once and for all, but cuts it straight away as it grows back, so too the word of God in us does not tear out, root and all, the movement of desire that is as though inborn in us (for perfect holiness is reserved for the age to come). Rather, it puts that movement to death as it grows back and springs up in us, and it tames the law that runs wild in the members of the flesh. So the removal of the hair hints at the cleansing of the mind, which the divine and sharper word of God works in us. And the washing of the garments points to a bright and genuine way of life for us, the one that is seen outwardly. For, as it is written, ‘taking thought for what is good, not only before the Lord but also before people’ (2 Corinthians 8:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shaving of the body and washing of garments.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The two calves, one burned whole as a fragrance and one slaughtered for sin, show the one Christ, wholly holy and slaughtered in innocence.
comments.comment: He said that the sacrifice for them must be offered with two calves, one full-grown and one a year old, that is, tender and young (Numbers 8:8). The full-grown one is for the whole burnt offering, and fine flour mixed with oil is burned together with it; the other, for sin, is burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:12), for that is how the sacrifices for sin are completed. And here again Christ is in both. In the calf for the whole burnt offering he is wholly holy and a sweet-smelling fragrance to God the Father on our behalf (Ephesians 5:2), bringing to the saints the delight and gladness of the life that is in hope; for the fine flour mixed with oil was offered up together with the calf, and it will surely, I think, follow those who have honored the life that is in Christ. He is also the young calf for sin, consumed by fire, for ‘by his wound we were healed’ (Isaiah 53:5), as the Scriptures say. Notice that the full-grown calf is burned whole, while the yearling is slaughtered for sin (Numbers 8:12), so that through the two you may understand at once the One: most fragrant in a spiritual sense, as in the perfection of virtues, and slaughtered, as in simplicity and innocence. For he says: ‘I, like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed, did not know’ (Jeremiah 11:19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The laying on of hands shows the people setting the Levites before God in their own place, and an ordination outside the church and the people's presence would be contrary to the divine will.
comments.comment: The laying on of hands by the people of Israel would show that the priestly race is brought to God as an offering on behalf of all and from all together. For he says: ‘The sons of Israel shall lay their hands on the heads of the Levites’ (Numbers 8:10). The Levites laid their hands on the heads of the sacrificial victims, which were slaughtered on their behalf as a type of Christ (Numbers 8:12). They did this not to bless them in any way, far from it, but as though by the laying on of hands to point to the God who bears our sins (Isaiah 53:4) and is offered in sacrifice for us, so that he might nail to his own cross the record of debt that stood against us (Colossians 2:14). You will understand that the people’s ordination of the Levites was carried out in the same way. For when they laid their hands on them, it was as though they were setting them before God in their own place for the sacred service, as chosen men. Then, the laying on of hands was the practice. But now that things have passed over to what is incomparably better, the people vote for those who are called through Christ to the sacred service, joining heartily in the cry that they are worthy; and they do this in the churches, just as, of course, those of old performed the laying on of hands upon the Levites at the sacred and divine tabernacle (Numbers 8:10). It is plain, then, that if an ordination took place neither in church nor in the presence of the people, it would be contrary to the divine will and outside the sacred laws.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the laying on of hands and why the people take part.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The one who feasts to God eats the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth with bitter herbs, as Paul did in toil, hunger and watchings.
comments.comment:
If 'narrow and afflicted is the way,' how does your feast come to be with bitter herbs? For when you feast, it says 'you shall eat unleavened breads upon bitter herbs.' (Exodus 12:8; Num 9:11) What the word wants saying that the one feasting to God must eat 'unleavened breads upon bitter herbs' (1 Corinthians 5:8) must be considered. The apostle interpreted the unleavened breads; the interpretation is not mine; but what follows of the interpretation must necessarily be near the apostolic interpretation.

The apostle interpreted the things about the unleavened breads saying: 'Let us feast not in old leaven nor in leaven of wickedness and evil, but in unleavened breads of sincerity and truth.' (1 Corinthians 5:8) It is necessary to give the account about the bitter herbs following upon the unleavened breads being of sincerity and truth. Have sincerity and truth, and bitter herbs will be yours, and you eat with bitter herbs the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth—as Paul. Since he ate the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? Saying 'I have become your enemy speaking truly to you.' How did he eat bitter herbs? 'In toil and labor, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, apart from the things besides.' (2 Corinthians 11:27–28)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Passover bread is eaten with bitter herbs.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Homilies on Jeremiah

comments.capsule: As the one who did not eat the Passover is destroyed and the destroyer cannot touch those who ate, so the one who eats the true sheep's flesh has life.
comments.comment: And let us see whether what has been said by the Savior follows what was said in the Passover. For as it was said there that the one who has not eaten the Passover shall be utterly destroyed from his people, so now he says of the true sheep that the one who has not eaten of his flesh does not have life. As there the destroyer cannot touch those who have eaten of the sheep, so now the one who has eaten of the true sheep flees the destroyer
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the one who does not eat the Passover is cut off.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Pascha

comments.capsule: The fire of night suits the infants who need illumination and the cloud suits those made bright by faith, and the Church follows Christ everywhere.
comments.comment: For this is the being seen as in a form of fire by night, yet in a form of cloud by day. For it was necessary, necessary for those still infants to have illumination and shining that carries off unto God-knowledge; yet for those above these and made bright through the faith, shelter and help, so that they might be able to carry through nobly the present life’s heat and the day’s burden: ‘For all who wish to live piously in Christ will be persecuted.’ (2 Timothy 3:12) And when the cloud sets out, the tent also sets out together, and when it settles it is set down together, and with it those from Israel were doing this; for the Church follows Christ everywhere, and the holy multitude of those believing is not separated from the one calling unto salvation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: The tent covered by the cloud is the Church, filled by Christ with his glory, who shines like fire on those in darkness and gives shade and shelter to the already enlightened.
comments.comment: The holy tent having been raised according to the desert, it says the cloud has filled it; then it commanded those from Israel to set out together and settle down together with it, charging them to make the observation of the settings-out up and down with much exactness, and showing from this that the transgression is precarious for those who wish to be slack. Yet these things historically. Let us already contemplate spiritually. For at once both the truest tent has been raised and has risen upon the earth—that is, the Church—it has been filled with Christ’s glory; for the ancient tent’s being covered with the cloud signals, I think somewhere, nothing other than this. Christ therefore has filled the Church with his own glory, and for those spending time in ignorance and wandering, as it were in night and darkness, he shines up in fire’s manner, clearly casting in the intelligible illumination; yet for those already illuminated, and having the intelligible day in heart, granting his own shade and shelter, and fattening them down with spiritual dews—that is, with the consolations from above and through the Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: Christ richly nourishes those who live in day and light and enlightens those less instructed, and in the Churches there is no darkness of worldly deceit.
comments.comment: When the cloud set out, the people set out with it; and when it halted, they camped with it (Numbers 9:17–18). ‘For the cloud,’ it says, ‘was over the tent by day, and fire by night’ (Exodus 40:38). For Christ richly nourishes with spiritual gifts those who have come to be, as it were, in day and light, because they have grasped the knowledge of him with precision and careful study and have had their minds made bright; and he enlightens those who are still less instructed. But in the Churches there is no darkness of worldly deceit at all, since Christ shines all around them and floods all things with spiritual light; for we are not of night or of darkness, but sons of light and of day, as it is written (1 Thessalonians 5:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the cloud by day and fire by night mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Only the priests are given the use of the trumpets, because the word that teaches and stirs up desire for virtue belongs to the trainers of the people.
comments.comment: And observe that he allots only to those who have obtained to be priests the using the trumpets; dedicating, I think somewhere, to the peoples’ trainers and those sanctified unto priesthood the word that mystagogues [leads into the mysteries], and indeed also that oils toward desire of virtue. For on account of this, I think, toward Moses he says: ‘Make for yourself two trumpets.’ (Numbers 10:2) And as it were sealing the matter by law: ‘And Aaron’s sons,’ he says, ‘the priests, will trumpet with the trumpets; and it will be for you an eternal lawful thing unto your generations.’ (Numbers 10:1–8)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: The ark going before Israel, and Moses' prayer at its lifting and resting, are types of Christ, who went up to the Father first and mediates for us.
comments.comment: Christ therefore was being typed beforehand as in the ark; for that one had been constructed from woods that do not rot, and was packing densely in itself the divine law, which is God’s Word. And you would see the mystery upon Christ resembling this. For the Word was God in an incorruptible temple. Therefore the ark was going forward reconnoitering the rest for those from Israel. And our Christ also goes forward according to the manners just now said to us; and besides this also filling the mediator’s need, he becomes advocate toward the Father, and propitiation on behalf of us, according as Moses also of old; who in the lifting of the ark was saying: ‘Rise up, Lord, let your enemies be scattered, let all who hate you flee;’ (Numbers 10:35) yet in the resting: ‘Return, Lord, thousands of myriads in Israel.’ (Numbers 10:36) For when the Only-begotten has been raised toward our help and the one who of old was saying through the Psalmist’s voice: ‘From the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy now I will rise, says the Lord;’ (Psalms 12:5) then the enemies have fallen, and those who have stood against and fight with the divine glory have fled. For he has triumphed in the cross over rulers and authorities; and having died he has abolished the ruler of this age, according to what has been written; and having as it were rested, and brought to an end the whole economy through the resurrection from dead ones and the journey upward toward the Father, he turned the whole earth, and was making thousands of myriads his own worshipers: ‘For when,’ he was saying, ‘I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all toward myself.’ (John 12:32) Therefore Moses’ prayer would be a type of Christ’s mediation, according at least to the human form, praying and asking for us the finest things from beside the God and Father. For as divine John says: ‘We have an advocate toward the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is propitiation concerning our sins, and not concerning ours only, but also on behalf of the whole world.’ (1 John 2:2)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: God overlooks wickedness growing for a time so that those who lust may be sated, see the harm and hate what they once welcomed, as with the mixed multitude who lusted for flesh.
comments.comment: Since, then, speedy healing, and more compendious, breeds in some a contempt of the diseases into which they fell — easily healed, so that after healing they would fall a second time into the same — reasonably, in such cases, he overlooks wickedness growing for a time, and, spreading longer in them, overlooks it as incurable: that, by spending time with evil and being glutted with the sin they desire, they may be sated, perceive the harm, hate what they formerly welcomed, and, healed, be able more firmly to profit from the health belonging to being healed in their souls. As the 'mixed multitude' 'among the sons of Israel 'lusted a lust, and, sitting down, the sons of Israel wept too, and said: Who shall feed us flesh? We remembered the fish we ate freely in Egypt, and the cucumbers and the melons and the leeks and the onions and the garlic. But now our soul is dry; nothing but the manna are our eyes.' (Numbers 11:4-6)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Prayer

comments.capsule: The seventy to be appointed are those already known to be elders, so that those who have acquired seniority are made manifest.
comments.comment: Concerning those having such a judgment, a polity, and a mental age, the Cause of all things and the Provider of all good things says to his faithful servant: 'Appoint with yourself seventy elders, whom you yourself know to be elders' (Numbers 11:16). … He shows those who are older not as those who were previously so, but makes them manifest. For it was strictly ordered that those whom the forerunner already knew to be such should be ordained.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
comments.work: Commentary on Zechariah

comments.capsule: God gave them the flesh they lusted for, for a whole month, so that the lust would not remain in them.
comments.comment: But the philanthropic and good God, giving them what they lusted for, did not so will to give as to leave lust remaining in them. That is why he says they shall eat the 'flesh' not 'one day' — for their passion would have remained in their soul, fired and kindled by it, if they had shared flesh for a little — nor 'two' days does he give them what they lusted for. Wishing to make it loathsome to them, he as it were promises not, but threatens the discerning through what he seemed to grant — saying: you shall not make 'five' days 'only' eating the 'flesh,' nor twice those, nor yet twice those — but 'you shall eat' so long, feasting on flesh a whole month, 'until it come out of your nostrils,' (Numbers 11:20)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: On Prayer

comments.capsule: At eighty Moses saw God as far as a human can, as God himself testifies, and so speaks to us from what he heard from God.
comments.comment: When he was already eighty years old, he saw God as far as it is possible for a human being to see—or rather, as it was granted to no one else, according to the very testimony of God: “If there is a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in sleep. Not so with my servant Moses; he is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in visible form, and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:6-8). This man, then, who was counted worthy of the face-to-face vision of God equally with the angels, speaks to us from what he heard from God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God's testimony about Moses means.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Moses, who fasted forty days and nights, saw God as no other human has, and fasting gave him the sight as a gift.
comments.comment: Moses fasted forty days and forty nights, entered that darkness, and saw God as has happened to no one among human beings, according to the testimony of God himself about him, saying: “If there is a prophet among you who belongs to the Lord, I will make myself known to him in a vision and speak to him in a dream. Not so with my servant Moses; mouth to mouth, face to face, as one speaks to his own friend” (Numbers 12:6-8). Fasting brought this extraordinary sight to the prophet as a gift, changed the face of the one who fasted into a kind of divine lightning-flash of unapproachable light, and gave the prophet tablets written by the finger of God.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: Homily on Fasting

comments.capsule: Faith in the sense of Moses being faithful in all his house means steadfastness toward every good thing and toward whatever God may will.
comments.comment: Faith here would be, as I think, steadfastness toward every good thing whatever, and toward whatever God may will. For in this sense we say that Moses, the revealer of holy things, was faithful “in all his house” (Hebrews 3:2; Numbers 12:7). For faith would not be understood or spoken of as only the duty to believe that by nature and in truth there is one God of all, but as standing firm in soul, “and being ready to walk with the Lord God,” in the words of the prophet (Micah 6:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Moses was faithful in all God's house.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: Fragments on 1 Corinthians

comments.capsule: The prophets spoke plainly what hearers could use at once but set forth the more mystical matters through riddles so that those who labor for virtue might search and find.
comments.comment: The prophets, then, in accordance with the will of God, spoke without any concealment whatever their hearers could usefully understand at once and whatever helped to correct their conduct. But what was more mystical, more for the eyes of the initiated, and bound up with a contemplation beyond what the common ear can take in, they set forth “through riddles” (Numbers 12:8), through allegories, through what are called dark sayings, and through what are named parables or proverbs (Proverbs 1:6). They did this so that those who do not shrink from toil, but take on every labour for the sake of virtue and truth, might examine and find, and, having found, might put what they found to use as reason requires.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God speaks to prophets in riddles.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
comments.work: Against Celsus, Book VII

comments.capsule: Leprosy is a deadening of the flesh that eats away more than most, which is why Moses was filled with fear and begged God to heal Miriam.
comments.comment: Now leprosy is a deadening of the flesh, and an affliction that eats away more than most. That is why the inspired Moses, when Miriam had become leprous, was filled with fear and deep distress, and pleaded, saying: ‘O God, I beg you, heal her’ (Numbers 12:13). For he said: ‘Let her not become like a stillborn child coming out of its mother’s womb, and it will eat away half of her flesh’ (Numbers 12:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Miriam's leprosy so alarmed Moses.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Miriam's punishment was to make the people fear, as no one will be spared.
comments.comment: When Miriam reviled Moses, she was struck with leprosy and sat outside the camp for seven days (Numbers 12:15). This happened for the fear of the people. For if he did not spare his sister, neither will he spare another.
